title: ‘Sense and Sensibility’ Costume Designer on Blending Historical Accuracy and Modern Styling for the Dashwood Sisters: ‘We Want to Do Jane Austen Justice’
description: “Sense and Sensibility” costume designer Grace Snell thought in chapters for Georgia Oakley’s new take on Jane Austen’s 1811 novel, starring Daisy
body:
“Sense and Sensibility” costume designer Grace Snell thought in chapters for Georgia Oakley’s new take on Jane Austen’s 1811 novel, starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles as Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, respectively.

	The most distinct chapters, from Snell’s costuming perspective, are the country and the city. First, the Barton Cottage chapter, shaped by the Devonshire landscape. There, behind closed doors, the relationship between the Dashwood sisters is at its most intimate. Then, the London chapter, where Elinor and Marianne’s presentation to society takes on a different palette. Snell says the sets, weather and changing seasons inspired her work in the different phases.
	

	Austen’s debut novel begins with the Dashwood family — sisters Elinor, Marianne, Margaret and their mother — settled at Norland Park, their Sussex estate. It’s set between the Georgian and Regency eras, in what Snell calls an “unusual transition period” as fashion began to “massively revolutionize” into the simpler style associated with Austen. Snell’s costuming inspiration, however, pulls from an array of eras, from period-accurate paintings and archival costume pieces to family portraits from the 2000s.


	In those photographs, “I really homed in on the intimacy that is within a family,” Snell says. “Particularly with sisters, and how relaxed and how comfortable they are with each other, and what that looks like in clothing.”

	One of Snell’s favorite details, and one she hopes fans pick up on, is that the sisters share clothing — emphasized by the Dashwood girls’ age gap. At the onset, Marianne is 19, Elinor is 16 and Margaret is 13.
	

	“There’s moments of borrowing because that’s what sisters do. They’re stealing clothes from each other. There’s being inspired by each other and reimagining clothing,” Snell says. “The dynamic of those sisters and how they share clothes and how they’re inspired by each other was important. We do rework some of the fabrics so that the garments look that they have a life themselves and how garments are loved and shared and borrowed within a family.”



	

					Illustration by Ruby Enticknap
									Grace Snell
	



	Inspired by those family photographs from the early aughts, as well as some runway looks from the ‘80s and ‘90s, Snell styled the film with a more modern take. Part of that was based on a desire to make the period piece feel more accessible.

	“What I wanted to do was design a film that I could see myself in, my friends in, my family in, try and knock down the wall that often is associated with period dramas,” Snell explains. “There’s sometimes this level of separation that you feel you’re looking at them on a pedestal, and I really wanted to open that up.”

	Still, “Sense and Sensibility” is not a modern film. Snell, who studied historical dress at university, brought a dress historian on board for three weeks of research. “I wanted how we made the costumes to be historically accurate with the fabrics we used, and the techniques we used, and the hand sewing,” she says. “For me as a designer, it was an amazing experience to try and fight those two sides, making historic accuracy marry up with how I wanted to give us a more modern take in the film.”

	The film’s colors were also chosen with care: “Sense and Sensibility” begins in a period of mourning, which formed “this idea of ‘shades of black.’” When the Dashwood sisters are in London, Elinor and Edward are both in shades of blue to reflect the disappointment of their situation. Snell used brighter colors in controlled ways, mainly for the supporting characters.



	

					Illustration by Ruby Enticknap
									Grace Snell
	



	“Sense and Sensibility” was Snell’s first period film, and she says part of the challenge was simply the volume of pieces. At the same time, she had to manage the entire costume team. There’s a lot to juggle, so the first challenge “is within yourself and your own head,” she says. “The biggest challenge is overcoming self-doubt.”
	

	Snell is a self-proclaimed Austen fan, so she understood how much of an undertaking this adaptation was. “I tried to not be intimidated by the fact that we were making a Jane Austen and how big a deal that was,” she says.

	This film looks different from Ang Lee’s 1995 adaptation, which Snell notes is a touchstone for many Austen fans. “I love that film. I have massive respect for [costume designers] Jenny Beavan and John Bright,” she says. But “it was not a reference point for the design. They were two separate things, but the weight of how much it’s a beloved film, obviously we have to acknowledge that there are going to be people that that is a film that has meant so much to them.”

	Rather than referring back to Lee and Emma Thompson, Snell brings it back to Austen herself. “We want to do Jane Austen justice,” she says. “I think it’s time to have our version of a human story, and see this level of intimacy between the sisters and have a new take on it. It’s important to keep reworking these stories. Jane Austen’s books are so timeless and so relevant today, and hopefully we reach a new audience as well with our film.”

schema.headline: ‘Sense and Sensibility’ Costume Designer on Blending Historical Accuracy and Modern Styling for the Dashwood Sisters: ‘We Want to Do Jane Austen Justice’

title: Gene Schwam, Veteran Hollywood Publicist to Elvis Presley, Julie Andrews and More, Dies at 96
description: Veteran Hollywood publicist Gene Schwam, who represented top talent including Elvis Presley, Blake Edwards, Julie Andrews, Barbara Eden and Lenny B
body:
Veteran Hollywood publicist Gene Schwam, who represented top talent including Elvis Presley, Blake Edwards, Julie Andrews, Barbara Eden and Lenny Bruce, died Friday in Los Angeles after a brief illness. He was 96.

	Schwam co-founded Hanson & Schwam Public Relations with Adeline Hanson in 1955, establishing an independent publicity agency that would endure for decades.

	Schwam was earning $35 a week working for publicist Stanley Cowan when he decided to strike out on his own. He joined forces with Hanson, a part-time disc jockey and publicist, to launch their firm. When it came time to decide whose name would come first, Schwam wanted his own name at the front. Hanson’s response settled the matter: “Ladies first.”
	

	Starting with Smith Bros. Fish Shanty restaurant as their first client, Hanson & Schwam grew into an enduring presence in entertainment publicity, with Schwam continuing as president and co-founder decades later. 


	Clients included Nancy Wilson and Lou Rawls, as well as the famous Coconut Grove nightclub, which helped the agency foster relationships with numerous entertainers.

	His colorful representation (and intentional misreputation) of Presley in 1957 was covered in Variety at the time of the release of Baz Luhrmann’s “Elvis” in 2022.Schwam’s longtime relationship with Edwards extended beyond the professional. He was a friend as well as a publicist to the legendary director of such classics as “Breakfast at Tiffany’s,” “10,” and“Victor/Victoria.”

	Edwards’ character of the neurotic publicist in his film “S.O.B.” was based on Schwam. That friendship reflected something fundamental about Schwam’s approach: he was known for his passionate engagement and resourceful guidance of his clients’ careers.

	Vernon Scott, the longtime United Press International entertainment correspondent, called him “The best idea man in Hollywood,” a description that captured the inventive thinking at the center of Schwam’s work. 
	

	Later in life, Schwam created Humanity 101, an initiative of Arizona State University’s Project Humanities, promoting the values of compassion, empathy, forgiveness, integrity, kindness, respect and self-reflection.

	He is survived by his wife, Myrna; daughter Stephanie Schwam (Instagram contact @youreprettyandnice); stepchildren Adam, Greg and Linda London; and four grandchildren.

schema.headline: Gene Schwam, Veteran Hollywood Publicist to Elvis Presley, Julie Andrews and More, Dies at 96

title: Harry Styles Debuts Unreleased Song He Wrote in Memory of Liam Payne, ‘What Is Enough,’ on Second Anniversary of Ex-Bandmate’s Death
description: The mood was typically celebratory at Harry Styles‘ residency show at New York’s Madison Square Garden Friday night, but Harry Styles was not about
body:
The mood was typically celebratory at Harry Styles‘ residency show at New York’s Madison Square Garden Friday night, but Harry Styles was not about to let the second anniversary of the death of former One Direction bandmate Liam Payne go unremarked upon — or, to the shock of fans, unsung about.

	Styles used the encore at MSG to premiere “What Is Enough,” a song he said he wrote “about two years ago” but has kept private until now. Performed as an acoustic ballad with minimal accompaniment, the number had Styles singing his thoughts aloud to Payne, to “help you understand what you leave behind.” In the lyrics, he further described the funeral that took place Nov. 20, 2024, singing, “I could tell you what it’s like to bury friends on a Wednesday night, gathered in the garden ’round a fire.”
	

	Fans who were in attendance or have seen video of the performance struggled to make out all the words, between the cavernous sound of the arena and Styles’ extreme soft-spokenness in delivering this musical eulogy. But among the touching lines that seemingly could be made out were such sentiments as: “Among the stars above, the friend in all those satellites… I’m not wise enough, but I wrote you a letter just to burn it up, and watch it rise.” 



	Styles backed into the song with a preamble that at first seemed just to be a “drive safely”-type goodnight message, before it turned out to be much more than that. “I hope you keep looking after each other, and please get home safety,” he said. “Tell a stranger you love ’em; tell your friends that you love ’em.”
	

	He then started reflecting on his history with the building.  ”Being here, I feel incredibly lucky to get to play these shows here in New York. This building means a lot to me, as I said, and I feel incredibly proud when I get to look up there and see my name up there from last year,” he said, acknowledging a banner celebrating his previous success with a “Together, Together” run of shows at MSG. “And there are so many people in my life, friends and people that I’ve worked with, that I wouldn’t have been able to do this without. And two years ago today, I lost one of those friends. It’s sad. I’m sure a lot of you have been through similar things. I hope you haven’t. But, really, it’s just about looking after each other. And there are so many people more than my name that is on that banner. There are so many more people behind it, so many people who have touched my life in such special ways. I wouldn’t be here without them.”

	To huge cheers, he then announced, “I’m gonna play you a song that I wrote for my friend about two years ago, if that’s all right with you… This is ‘What Is Enough.'”

	Following the surprising premiere, Styles returned to the show’s regularly scheduled programming, rounding out the encore with “Sign of the Times” and “Aperture.”

schema.headline: Harry Styles Debuts Unreleased Song He Wrote in Memory of Liam Payne, ‘What Is Enough,’ on Second Anniversary of Ex-Bandmate’s Death

title: How NBC Brought Live Musicals Back to Television
description: In 2011, NBC was in a rough shape. The network had struggled in the waning years under General Electric’s ownership. In January 2011, Comcast becam
body:
In 2011, NBC was in a rough shape. The network had struggled in the waning years under General Electric’s ownership. In January 2011, Comcast became the majority shareholder, and with it came a new leadership regime for NBC Entertainment, led by industry veteran Bob Greenblatt.

	One of Greenblatt’s big ideas to liven up NBC’s schedule was to lean in to the network’s roots as the home of great entertainment specials and spectacles. NBC carried what was a landmark moment for Broadway on TV in March 1955 with its live telecast of Mary Martin performing her signature role in the beloved Comden and Green tuner. It was a smash in the Trendex ratings of the day.
	

	Greenblatt’s experience as a Broadway producer gave him the confidence to take on “The Sound of Music Live” with the help of veteran producers Craig Zadan and Neil Meron. Carrie Underwood was cast as Maria, Stephen Moyer was tapped as Capt. Von Trapp. The “Sound of Music” team spent money and time setting up an elaborate made-for-live-TV production that would be beamed live from a Grumman Studios soundstage on Long Island.


	Nobody — not even Greenblatt, Zadan or Meron — quite knew what NBC had until the opening moments of the production on Dec. 5, 2013. Within minutes, fans ranging from Tina Fey to Cameron Diaz to everyday people who love tuners were chiming in on Twitter with posts noting the joy of singing along with the beloved Rodgers and Hammerstein standard.

	RELATED STORY: From Bob Hope to Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade to ‘Wicked: One Wonderful Night’: How NBC Became America’s Home for TV Specials
	

	Greenblatt credits the late producer Zadan and his longtime partner Meron for picking “Sound of Music” as the one to roll the dice on.

	“They thought it could bring in a huge audience since it’s beloved by adults and children and is constantly being produced all over the world,” Greenblatt says. “We had no idea how to even produce a live musical or how we could market it since it there hadn’t been anything like it in decades. But everyone at the network got excited about it and came together to turn it into a powerhouse.”

	“Sound of Music Live” delivered an astounding 18 million-plus viewers — well past the hope internally that it would reach at least 10 million. It became a milestone in NBC’s revival, and it revved up the strategy to emphasize crowd-pleasing live events to reinforce the network’s prominence as a platform that reaches every corner of the U.S.

	The success of “Sound of Music” allowed NBC to produce four more live tuners during Greenblatt’s time at the helm of the network. (There was one that got away — a planned production of “Bye Bye Birdie” toplined by Jennifer Lopez never came to fruition in 2017.)

	“Peter Pan Live,” starring Allison Williams and Christopher Walken. Airdate: Dec. 2, 2014

	“The Wiz Live,” starring Queen Latifah, David Alan Grier and ingenue Shanice Williams. Airdate: Dec. 3, 2015

	“Hairspray Live,” starring Marissa Jaret Winokur and Derek Hough. Airdate: Dec. 7, 2016

	“Jesus Christ Superstar Live in Concert,” starring John Legend and Sara Bareilles. Airdate: April 1, 2018

	Here’s a look at Variety’s coverage, starting with a ratings report for the original 1955 “Peter Pan” presentation with Mary Martin. This clip — which notes that NBC’s “two-hour colorcast” walloped the competition, sending CBS’ “I Love Lucy” to an all-time low rating — ran on March 9, 1955, two days after NBC’s triumph.



	

					From the March 9, 1955, edition of Daily Variety
	



	“The Sound of Music Live!” caught the TV industry by surprise, as noted in this report from Dec. 13, 2013. The program earned six Emmy nominations (and one win) as the it pushed the envelope on live music production, as covered in this story from Aug. 12, 2014.



	

					From the Dec. 13, 2013, edition of Variety
	





	

					“The Sound of Music Live” on NBC in 2013
									NBC/NBCU Photo Bank
	



	“The Sound of Music Live” nabbed six Emmy nominations and one win. The artistry of the presentation was examined in this story that ran Aug. 12, 2014.



	

					From the Aug. 14, 2014, edition of Variety
	



	The following year, there was much more buildup to the production of “Peter Pan Live,” including a Variety set visit preview story that ran Nov. 25, 2014.



	

					From the Nov. 25, 2014, edition of Variety
	





	

					“Peter Pan Live” in 2014
									NBC/NBCU Photo Bank
	



	Variety also was there the following year for the final dress rehearsal of “The Wiz,” as covered in this report published on the morning of the live telecast in 2015.



	

					“The Wiz Live” in 2015
									NBC/NBCU Photo Bank
	



	“Hairspray Live” may have been set in Baltimore but it was produced out of the Universal lot in North Hollywood. Once again, Variety was there for this curtain-raiser story published on Dec. 7, 2016.



	

					“Hairspray Live” in 2016
									NBC/NBCU Photo Bank
	



	“Jesus Christ Superstar Live” marked a moment of triumph for the aptly-named John Legend, who gave his all in the lead role to entertain and inspire America on Easter Sunday 2018. The technical feats of the production were chronicled in this Variety Artisans preview report from March 25, 2018.



	

					From the March 25, 2018, edition of Variety
	





	

					“Jesus Christ Superstar Live in Concert” in 2018
									NBC/NBCU Photo Bank
	



	The chance to bring a bit of Broadway-style razzle-dazzle to the airwaves was extremely gratifying to Greenblatt, who produced the Broadway tuner “9 to 5: The Musical” with Dolly Parton in 2009 and has been involved with many other shows. The buzz NBC generated with its adventurous live productions inspired other networks embrace the form — the sincerest form of flattery in TV. Fox staged live renditions of “Grease” in 2016 and “Rent” in 2019.

	“I was gratified that our big risk paid off, and I think the live musicals have become part of NBC’s [modern] legacy alongside Must-See TV, Dick Wolf dramas and the Olympics,” Greenblatt says. “The other networks jumped on board too, which was the best sign of success.”

	Greenblatt’s time at NBC ended in the fall of 2018. The five live musical productions that the network delivered on his watch are among his proudest accomplishments. And he’s not done yet.

	“At this very moment, I’m talking to NBC and ABC about producing a brand new live musical,” Greenblatt says. “Long may they live!”

schema.headline: How NBC Brought Live Musicals Back to Television

title: ‘You Can See Everything’: That Shocking, Meta Twist With [SPOILER] Explained in Elizabeth Holmes Doc
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “You Can See Everything,” now playing in theaters.

	About halfway through Nathan Fielder a
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “You Can See Everything,” now playing in theaters.

	About halfway through Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything,” the film’s shock value ratchets up yet again. Even after a full-frontal scene from Holmes’ boyfriend Billy Evans and the convicted fraudster claiming she’s never told a lie, the movie dials it up to 11 with a meta appearance by actress Amanda Seyfried.
	

	Seyfried memorably played the Theranos founder in Hulu’s 2022 series “The Dropout,” which Fielder shows Holmes and Evans for the first time — though it brings the real-life subject to tears. The documentary chronicles the 34 days ahead of Holmes’ 11-year prison sentence, and then Fielder introduces the Seyfried twist halfway through the film after Holmes is incarcerated.


	Fielder recruits Seyfried to get her take on some of his odd interactions with Holmes once she’s gone, given that the actress won an Emmy for playing her on “The Dropout.” The meta-ness of Seyfried returning to play Holmes snowballs into her reenacting real-life moments that Fielder and Oppenheim couldn’t capture on camera. Alongside her is “East of Eden” actor Christopher Abbott, who plays Evans, albeit with a smaller role than Seyfried (who goes on to become a main character of the final half). 

	The two actors recreate a private negotiation between Fielder, Oppenheim and the A24 team that happened before filming for “You Can See Everything” commenced. In it, Seyfried (as Holmes) leaves the conversation to tend to her child, and Abbott (as Evans) demands that he be paid for participating in the documentary. Fielder and Oppenheim (as themselves) push back, arguing that paying the couple would severely discredit the film, but A24 relents and agrees to pay them. 
	

	The question then looms over the rest of the film: Did Holmes intentionally leave the room to have deniability on the sketchy payment, or did Evans go rogue and request the money by himself, leaving Holmes out of it? Fielder eventually visits Holmes in prison, where she says she didn’t know about the payment (which we later see recreated in a scene with Seyfried). At the end of the movie, it’s also revealed that Evans dropped his financial request, without further explanation.

	In what is perhaps the film’s most meta moment, Seyfried (as Holmes) tells Fielder during their off-camera prison visit, “I don’t want that to happen ever again,” referencing “The Dropout.” In the conversation, Holmes rants about how awful it is that women would “do that” to other women, making a point that Seyfried and the entire “Dropout” team is at fault. She adds that so many of the women incarcerated with her believe that “The Dropout” depicted entirely real events. 

	Intercut with Seyfried playing Holmes in the prison visit, we see the actress (as herself) reading the script Fielder prepared with his actual conversation from Holmes. Reading Holmes’ accusations, Seyfried’s guard is immediately up. The actress argues that she “didn’t do that to [Holmes]. She did that to herself,” later adding, “it’s not lies. It’s fucking TV.”

	Fielder, ever the documentarian, pushes back, questioning whether Seyfried’s scenes in “The Dropout” were completely accurate. Seyfried, still defensive, acknowledges she doesn’t know exactly what happened in Holmes’ life, but that the Theranos founder’s behavior led to assumptions about her, and that’s not Seyfried’s or the show’s fault. This aligns with something Seyfried says earlier in the film: “We’re working in fiction-land” but with “ridiculous amounts of research,” including 10 hours of deposition tapes that she referenced to prepare for her 2022 role.

	Earlier in the doc, Seyfried told Fielder she will “reenact whatever you want me to reenact.” Fielder gently reminds her that she’s “not [Holmes],” prompting the actress to ask, “Guess how many people believed I was her when I played her?” She answers with a smile: “A lot.”

	Through it all, Seyfried struggles to decipher Holmes. On one hand, she’s empathetic, noting that no woman would want to see another woman in a relationship with someone as manipulative as Evans. But on the other hand, she can’t quite tell whether Holmes is duping everyone — again — creating a push-and-pull between the actress and the imprisoned woman.
	

	Viewers are also left wondering how authentic the film is. Fielder claims Seyfried’s re-created scenes are made using Holmes’ real speech, but we see Fielder develop a warmth toward Holmes. Seyfried questions if Fielder is protecting Holmes by showing a kinder depiction of her with their reenacted scenes. Is Fielder’s kinship with Holmes genuine, or is he playing a heightened version of himself in order to cast doubt on Holmes’ intentions?

	The movie ends on a quote from a New York Times interview with Holmes about “The Dropout”: “They’re not playing me. They’re playing a character I created.” It’s a contentious quote for Holmes, who, throughout the film, asserts that the New York Times misquoted her, who claims she said “a character they created” rather than the attributed “I.” The Times reporter has maintained that the quote is accurate. That single, hotly debated word makes all the difference, and viewers are left to wonder whether the on-camera version of Holmes we see is the real deal or a fictionalized dramatization of the real-life woman.

title: Miley Cyrus Tears Up While Honoring Dolly Parton During Hollywood Bowl Show: ‘Nothing In This Life Could Ever Tear Us Apart’
description: Miley Cyrus paid tribute to her late godmother and country icon Dolly Parton onstage at the Hollywood Bowl Friday as she performed her first major
body:
Miley Cyrus paid tribute to her late godmother and country icon Dolly Parton onstage at the Hollywood Bowl Friday as she performed her first major show in years.

	The “Bass Persuades” singer began by sharing memories with Parton, telling the audience she was partly inspired to play the venue because it was where she saw her godmother perform. 

	“Like so many things Dolly did that I didn’t understand at the time, sitting here with you all right now, feeling her all around me, knowing that she’s right here beside me every day, all the time, more than she could be when she was here, I feel her more than ever,” she said, getting emotional. “And knowing that I get to share this story with you all, it makes that night very worth it. This memory is gold to me. Me and Dolly, we are eternal. Nothing in this life could ever tear us apart. And I’m going to see her again, and I can’t fucking wait because I miss her.”
	

	Cyrus then performed “Jolene,” the classic country song Parton first released in 1974. “Some of the greatest music that we have today was written, produced and performed by my aunt Dolly,” she said. “This is one of those moments.” 


	Parton died Aug. 25 after a “brief battle” with cancer. The family’s official obituary said, “A rhinestone life that shone bright enough for the world to see, Dolly will forever stand as an inspiration not only through her timeless music and prolific songwriting, but also her wit, warmth, and kindness that made us all feel like family. Dolly Parton’s legacy is one of love, compassion, and resilience. With a seven-decade career, she inspired multiple generations of artists and fans with her music and an unwavering commitment to making the world a better place. Her songs will continue to resonate with people of all ages, and her philanthropic work will have a lasting impact.”
	

	Following her death, Cyrus shared an emotional tribute to Instagram. “The feeling of losing my Aunt Dolly is beyond what feels right to share. Our most sacred moments were private and they’ll stay there behind the stage, beneath the glamour & between our hearts,” Cyrus wrote. “What I KNOW is Dolly would want me to feel it, write a song about it, and then continue on and be strong. I have an angel by my side. I always have. One of our last conversations was about music and metamorphosis.”

schema.headline: Miley Cyrus Tears Up While Honoring Dolly Parton During Hollywood Bowl Show: ‘Nothing In This Life Could Ever Tear Us Apart’

title: Law Roach Wants to Try Acting: ‘If I’m Terrible at It, at Least I Tried’
description:
Law Roach is ready for an even bigger close-up.

	The celebrity stylist, whose clients include Zendaya, Kim Kardashian and Celine Dion, says he’s “
body:
Law Roach is ready for an even bigger close-up.

	The celebrity stylist, whose clients include Zendaya, Kim Kardashian and Celine Dion, says he’s “absolutely” ready to try some acting.

	“When a director sees something for me,” Roach told me Thursday night at the InStyle Imagemaker Awards. “I want to try everything. If I’m terrible at it, at least I tried.”


	He’s certainly worked with enough A-list actors to get some guidance, no? “I’ve also worked with some of the greatest singers of all time, but that doesn’t mean I’m going to try to sing,” Roach cracked.
	


	Roach has made cameos as himself in “The Devil Wears Prada 2” and the Kate Hudson Netflix sitcom “Running Point.” He has also served as reality television judge on “Legendary,” “America’s Next Top Model,” “Project Runway” and “RuPaul’s Drag Race.”



	

					Priyanka Chopra Jonas in Matières Fécales at the 2026 InStyle Imagemaker Awards.
									Variety via Getty Images
	



	Also on the carpet, fellow Imagemaker honoree (and sometimes Roach client) Priyanka Chopra Jonas talked about reuniting with her “Baywatch” co-star Zac Efron for “Judgment Day,” the upcoming Nicholas Stoller Amazon MGM Studios comedy that also stars Will Ferrell, Regina Hall and Fortune Feimster.

	“I had a blast. I went in there to learn and had a great time,” Jonas said. “I’m just sitting there and watching everyone.”


	Efron stars as a newly released prison inmate who takes a TV courtroom judge and his television cast and crew hostage. The cast also includes Michael Peña, Billy Eichner, Jimmy Tatro, Heidi Gardner, Bobby Cannavale and Bill Camp.
	

	Was Jonas breaking all the time? “No, no, I’m a professional,” she quipped. “Maybe twice. Once with Will, for sure and once with Regina. She said something and I was just done. Fortune said something too and I was really trying hard … I’m a girl that comes from drama, so to be surrounded by all of these amazing comedians and actors who are so easy with comedy, it was so cool to witness.”

schema.headline: Law Roach Wants to Try Acting: ‘If I’m Terrible at It, at Least I Tried’

title: 50 Cent Opens Up About Diddy’s Secret Smear Campaign Against Him, Why He Won’t Work With Courtney Kemp Again and Learning His Mom Was Gay: ‘I’m Not Ashamed of That in Any Way’
description: 50 Cent is having trouble logging in to our Zoom. Multiple links have been sent his way — three, by my count — to no avail. The imbroglio is excusab
body:
50 Cent is having trouble logging in to our Zoom. Multiple links have been sent his way — three, by my count — to no avail. The imbroglio is excusable given the early hour and the number of different directions he’s currently being pulled, with 40 projects spread across 12 different networks, not to mention the podcasts, movies and revitalizing the city of Shreveport, Louisiana, home to his G-Unit Films and Television studio. We must chat via Zoom because 50 is back home in Houston, Texas, having decamped from his native New York City in 2021.
	

	“I’m trying to get it together over here!” he explains upon entering the video chat. “For a second there we were experiencing technical difficulties.”


	The occasion for the chat is “Street Fighter,” a new blockbuster film adaptation of the popular video game series. Directed by Kitao Sakurai (“Bad Trip”), the film centers Ryu (Andrew Koji) and his adoptive brother Ken (Noah Centineo), two seasoned fighters who are recruited by Chun-Li (Callina Liang) to enter a World Warrior tournament held by the dictator M. Bison (David Dastmalchian), who has designs on extracting Ryu’s fighting power for personal gain. 50 plays Balrog, a boxer who works for Bison with a distinctive hi-top fade and pointed-front hairdo. The character was modeled after Mike Tyson; and to get into fighting shape, 50 trained three hours a day for nine weeks, dropping from 238 pounds to 200 pounds. “And no, I didn’t do no weight-loss shot!” he exclaims.

	These days, 50 — who is now 51 — is more business magnate than hip-hop artist, presiding over a sprawling TV empire that includes the “Power” universe and “Fightland” on Starz, and eye-opening documentaries like the Emmy-winning Netflix docuseries “Sean Combs: The Reckoning,” that exposed the evils of the artist sometimes known as Diddy. He’s also prepping a Hulu docuseries on himself.
	

	He spoke about it all, from Trump and Diddy to the tragic loss of his mom and why he won’t work with “Power” showrunner Courtney Kemp again (along with her response), in a no-holds-barred interview with Variety.
	
		This is how I know you’re more businessman than rapper now: I’ve never done a 9 a.m. interview with a rapper.	

	Right? They’re not even up and functioning from last night!
	
		Let’s start with “Street Fighter.” How did you accomplish that hairdo for Balrog?	

	Haha! I started playing with the idea of it ahead of time with my barber, and we decided there was no way to do it without cutting back into my hairline to create the outline of where [the hair piece] goes. It was tough keeping it in place once we started the fight scenes. They were doing touch-ups all the time. When I got ready to get out of there, I had no facial hair and no nothing! I was like, yo, I have to do Vegas tomorrow!
	
		You got pretty ripped for the movie. You looked like aughts 50.	

	You know what’s crazy? I have to lose weight to look intensely in shape. I’ve got it, it’s just under the stuff. Some people fight their way up to gain mass, but I fight my way down. I can look like security, bro. I get big. You’re going to see me soon looking big in another action-film project that I’m going to work on.
	
		There’s a “Many Men” needle drop in “Street Fighter.” Was that your idea?	

	That was the idea of the producer Cale [Boyter], who was cool. The character is based on Mike Tyson, and anybody who knows Mike knows that if it wasn’t boxing for him, it would have been armed robbery. That’s just who he was with the level of aggression that came out of Brownsville. So, my character is just coming out of jail and able to be in the tournament with the rest of them. He wants to fight everywhere.



	

					50 Cent as Balrog in “Street Fighter.”
									Paramount Pictures
	


	
		You have strange connections to Mike Tyson. Not only did you buy his gigantic house in Connecticut, which ended up being a huge money suck, but isn’t it true that the guy who shot you nine times, Darryl “Hommo” Baum, was Tyson’s friend and bodyguard?	

	Mike dedicated his fight [in June 2000 against Lou Savarese] to “Hommo.” But Mike wasn’t aware what happened. That’s just what they do at home. My connections to Mike are my connections to the street. I clashed with Jimmy Henchman and Mike had connections to Jimmy, too. When Mike started seeing me in places, he would look at me [knowingly] and go, “Yo,” like 50 is the real deal and the real shit right there. One time, I was going into the casino and ran into Mike and he told me, “50, I’m glad you’re with him, but he’s not going to know when to stop [spending]. He’s me.” He was talking about Floyd [Mayweather]. And you see Floyd’s financial state now, and he kind of did what Mike did with the finances.
	
	
		Floyd screwed you too, right? On your boxing promotion company TMT?	

	But I love him. He’s like a brother, and we never needed each other. We are our own separate entities that have established ourselves in different ways. There were benefits to me being around at the time, since he didn’t have the social following that he has now. He would say, “Tell 5 to post this and it’s going to be all over the place!” He was sending me the blurb of what he wanted out there, so I’d post it and then it’d be all over the place. But we connected even prior to my success in music. He flew his entire entourage to Puerto Rico to see me in 2002, even before “Get Rich or Die Tryin.’” He knew I was going to be the biggest thing in music.
	
		And you were an amateur boxer starting at 11 and continued it through your teenage years. Did you initially want to be a pro boxer?	

	I did. I think I live vicariously through [Mayweather] in the sense of not just being a fighter but being the best fighter. Boxing isn’t a sport you can play. You can play basketball, football and baseball, but in boxing, if you’re losing and getting your ass whooped, you’re just not good enough and not on the level. Each time you get out of the ring punch-drunk you have a personal epiphany about what you’re doing! You think, “Fuck it, I could do construction. I don’t need to be doing this shit.”
	
		I heard that you accidentally cracked your co-star Noah Centineo in the face?	

	Yeah! I worked for 30 days with the boxing trainer they had in Australia even before we started working with the stunt crew, so the moves were programmed in my system. We rehearsed it at half-speed and then bop-bop! I think it’s because he was doing so many stunts in the movie, so he didn’t slip and the punch just got him. I was like, “My bad, bro! You didn’t move!” He was like, “Oh, shit. All right. Come on, it’s OK.” And we just went right back into doing it. But that was a crazy moment, and I felt bad because it’s rare that I actually like everyone involved in a project, but I had fun with these people and I’d go back and do it again in a heartbeat. Cody [Rhodes] got a yacht for the whole cast for one weekend while we were in Australia and I rented out an amusement park and took the entire cast and crew as well as their loved ones.
	



	

					50 Cent, executive producer Courtney Kemp and Joseph Sikora on the set of “Power.”
									©Starz! Movie Channel/Courtesy Everett Collection
	


	
		You said it’s rare that you actually like everyone on a project. Is there anyone you clashed with so bad that you’d never work with them again?	

	Courtney [Kemp]. I don’t look forward to working with her ever again. I don’t think that she’s wholeheartedly a bad person, I just think that it got out of control for her. After the success of “Power,” she would go, “I wrote it.” Well, you did write it, but I uploaded everything that you wrote, and we got a “no” from everybody before we got a “yes,” and I wrote songs that captured, at its nucleus, each one of the leads that we had and that emotionally captured energy for scenes. When we went to pitch “Power” to Chris Albrecht [then-CEO of Starz], we’d pitch the show and then we would play a minute and 30 seconds of a song, and then we’d pitch the show and play another minute and 30 seconds of a song. I produced eight songs that went into it, including the theme song.
	
		So, you feel she was minimizing your contributions to the show?	

	I think she forgot. Because in the beginning, the sell for the show was “50 Cent.” That’s it. There was a point with Albrecht where I was like, “Y’all know what time it is, and I’ll tell you when the show comes back on.” And then Starz watched 40% of their subscribers disappear. They called me in to the office to talk about it, and said, “What kind of partner does this?!” I said, “You guys have been doing this a lot longer than I have, and I want to be clear that if you’re not identifying that you have a programming issue, then I don’t know what to say to you. Me saying, ‘Y’all know what time it is, and I’ll tell you when the show comes back on” means that you have nothing else on this network that people want to watch. They’ll cancel the subscription and then come back when it’s back on.” So, then I pitched them the “Power” universe. They didn’t want the “Power” universe; I forced the “Power” universe on them when they saw the forty percent decrease. It opened the idea up to them of, “Oh, let’s put some more of it on so we can force the subscribers to stay.” And it put me in a different position where they were like, “Oh… He can fuck us up and turn this shit off.”
	
	
		Now that’s power.	

	It made them see things a little bit differently. Chris [Albrecht] is such an innovative thinker that he saw the opportunity to make it great. And the budgeting for the original “Power” had gotten so fuckin’ high that the show cost nearly $12 million an episode. All the clothes you saw weren’t being sent. Every single clothing item on the show was being purchased three times. I was like, “What the fuck are you doing that for? They need to promote the clothing company.”

	When it came time to do “BMF” and the different shows, I lowered the budget because I had the clothing companies giving us clothes for promotional purposes, since they’ll get ten million eyeballs on it. There was all kinds of weird shit going on, but it got to a point where Courtney was trying to run the entire network through one show. She also said she didn’t want to do “Raising Kanan” because she didn’t want to tell a story where they already know the ending. Half the shit she was saying just didn’t make sense. I told her, “This is the late-‘80s going into the ‘90s, and that was the golden era for the drug trade.” Sascha [Penn] was able to make a masterpiece out of it that ran for five seasons. 

	(In a statement to Variety, Kemp responded: “While 50’s recollection of budgets and production requirements is uninformed, as he was rarely in a budget meeting, I have never once understated his importance in the genesis of ‘Power.’ While he did not write nor create the series, he was a large part of its birth. That said, I am completely bewildered by his need to mention me in interviews or podcasts. I have completely moved on in my career, and I hope that the imminent success of ‘Street Fighter’ allows him to do the same.”)
	
		I want to talk about “Sean Combs: The Reckoning.” That project had such a huge global impact that resulted in real-life consequences.	

	I wasn’t surprised. When it came to the Diddy doc, I had started it six months before I was able to get Alex Stapleton, the showrunner. And it’s important to understand that she is the reason why it’s great. It could have been over-aggressive where it felt like you’re attacking the person, but she used people’s perspectives to tell their truth. And what he did was actually worse than what’s in the doc.
	



	

					Alexandria Stapleton and Curtis “50 Cent” Jackson of “Sean Combs: The Reckoning.” 
									Getty Images for Netflix
	


	
		What do you feel was left out of the doc that was even worse?	

	When you look at the Cassie situation, people think of just the hallway [attack]. But you have to look at what transpired that made it get to that point where you’re kicking her on the floor, and where it didn’t even matter to him what he did to her. He also got in the habit of not paying people — even his artists, where he raked them and took their publishing — and he used that as a form of control.
	
		I still can’t believe he allegedly blew up Kid Cudi’s car. I mean, Cudi seems like the last person you’d want to blow up. That’s just crazy, man.	

	And what was that for? That was for his dealings with Cassie. [Diddy] had the habit of dealing with someone else’s woman. Like, every woman you’ve seen him with was with someone from celebrity culture prior to him, including Cassie who was with Ryan Leslie. He kind of took her from Ryan Leslie. And his choices are not by chance. He picks the person based on who they were with prior. He needed confirmation of his success through who they were with prior to him.
	
		So, I heard that he sent you a funeral wreath of flowers to the club E11even in Miami? My friend Rob manages E11even. What happened there? Were you sitting there getting a lap dance and then all of a sudden someone delivers you a funeral wreath?	

	Haha! I know Rob. They sent a bouquet of flowers over and I thought, “OK, I know where that came from.”
	
		Did it come with a note?	

	It didn’t have anything crazy on the note, but it was definitely for me.
	
		Is that the extent of the threats Diddy’s made toward you over the doc?	

	There were things that didn’t surface publicly that were attempts from him to damage the perception of me. He had people saying things about his activities that went back years and years, and these things didn’t surface until they removed the statute of limitations from sexual-assault allegations. Recently, he had a law firm that pulled away from him after [his accusers] had the ability to move forward with a lawsuit against him, which is weird because usually law firms will take their 30% contingency in the case. That same law firm has sixty sexual-assault cases for him. And it’s been two years already. Imagine responding to each of those lawsuits? That’s probably $150,000 a piece, or $9 million total. So, when he saw the $9 million bill, he probably went, “I didn’t agree to that bill!” The law firm is probably going to end up suing him.
	
	
		I wanted to go back to what you said about Diddy making attempts to damage the perception of you. What sort of stuff was he trying to spread?	

	He was trying to find people to make frivolous accusations against me. From his perspective, it was, “How do I cloud what’s going to happen to me?” You hear him on the phone in the doc saying he needed people in the media to help him discredit everybody else.
	
		I don’t think “Sean Combs: The Reckoning” has gotten enough credit for the recent conviction of Duane “Keffe D” Davis for his role in Tupac’s murder. The doc really helped get that story in front of a lot of eyeballs.	

	It does feel like that because it was the best presentation of it. But look, it wasn’t top secret, bro. He was saying that stuff in books. That information was clear and out there. The problem with getting away with things is that the person feels they can get away with anything, so then they regress further and do something later that turns into their downfall. It’s rare that people get away with things and then decide not to do those things again. It makes you feel like you have the power to get away with shit, so you do more shit like try to blow up Kid Cudi’s car. And where’s the police report for the car blowing up? Where are the police reports for people getting shot in the studio?

	Now, Netflix has such a wide reach that this went global. And international folks feel that if 50 is saying it, this is going to be the real hip hop insider shit that goes on. You know how important real is to hip hop and youth culture. These kids now will tell you who they shot last week and create a visual picture of the crime scene.


	
		That got Bobby Shmurda in trouble.	

	Yeah. A few guys out there wrote shit that was so accurate, I was like, “Damn! You just told on yourself! What the fuck is that?!” I was writing about stories I’d experienced, but those were situations in the past.
	
		Not “Mitch caught a body ‘bout a week ago.”	

	Yeah.
	
		One of my favorite stories about you is the time you bought 200 tickets on Groupon for $3,000 to a Ja Rule concert in Texas so that the first few rows would be completely empty.	

	The tickets were going for that cheap on Groupon! I said, “I want those first three rows.” I know what it feels like when they put the crowd too far back, so since it’s all digital, I saw that I got all the tickets but maybe four in the first three rows.
	
	
		Will Ja Rule be appearing in your upcoming Hulu docuseries about yourself?	

	Probably a small portion of it. There will be certain things that we talk about. It’s really less important to my life than people see it. In the docuseries, you’ll see me get emotional at points, but usually about what happened before. The loss of my mom — that is where I was the most confused and vulnerable.
	
		You were only eight years old.	

	Yeah. So, you’ve got to imagine when you only really have her — since I didn’t know my dad at all — when they tried to explain to me, “Your mom is gone, and she’s not coming back,” I was like, “No, she’s going to come back.” I couldn’t even process it at that point. And then I stayed at my grandmother’s. All that was rough, so we’ll reflect back on that and also talk about other stuff. When I got shot is not the first time I’d been shot at, or me shooting at other people.
	
		What was it like to find out your mom was a lesbian, and how did that shape your view of the LGBT community?	

	Marlow, look: When your mom has friends around, you look at them and just see friends. And how often does a woman have a female friend that she’s close to that she talks with often? As a child, I just saw two women hanging out. My grandmother informed me later that there was more going on and they weren’t just friends, and I was like, “Oh! Now I know what that was!” I’m not ashamed of that in any way. I grew up around that. I used vulnerability at the time I explained it, going, “Coming up I was confused, my mommy kissing a girl / Confusion occurs comin’ up in the cold world.”
	
		On “Hate It or Love It.”	

	Yeah. Other people have those things in their experience and their upbringing, but they leave it out because they don’t think that’s “cool.” I didn’t care about being vulnerable — it made it more powerful for me because I know someone else has had that experience and would understand it.
	
		Have you and Jay-Z ever talked about this? Because he also found out later in life that his mother is a lesbian.	

	No, but it is something we have in common.
	
		It is interesting that two of the biggest hip hop artists of our time have gay moms.	

	But then, find the line. We just reacted differently to it. One of us doesn’t mind, and the other one kind of minds a little bit.
	
	
		You are mighty prolific. Are there any unannounced projects you have in development that you can share with Variety?	

	I have 40 shows across 12 different networks, and 10 are going toward air. I completed 18 episodes of “Power: Origins” that are coming and also released “Fightland,” which was my first international show since it was U.K.-based, and am preparing for the second season of it. We still didn’t get the nod yet, but I think the success of the project commands that. I’ve seen the numbers. There’s my own doc at Hulu that we’re working on and a heap of other projects. There’s “Cash Kings,” which two networks want, and then “Bone Parish” at Starz, along with “Billion Dollar Lawyer” and “Power: Legacy.”
	
		They’ve just got to rename Starz the Curtis “50 Cent” Jackson Network at this point.	

	Haha. And then Peacock has an adaptation of my book “The Accomplice,” which will star Taraji P. Henson. I got the dream cast and crew that I wanted for that one.
	
		I’m getting the wrap, so lastly, Trump has offered you millions to perform at/or attend his rallies, but you’ve turned him down every time. And that’s easy money that you’ve turned down.	

	People make interesting choices, and sometimes you don’t know why they’re doing it. I think it’s a lack of a clear understanding of everything that’s going on. I try to stay as purple as possible, you know what I’m saying? I don’t understand things that are going on from the Democratic side at points, and then I don’t understand some of the mentality that’s connected to the Republican side. I think when people get ready to actually vote, they do it based on what’s affecting them. But I don’t have beef with nobody, especially in that realm. When you start to do big business, it becomes political because you see the state or local government provide aid for it since it will employ a lot of people. What can start out as a project for the studios can become a whole revitalization of a city.
	
		Like what you’re doing in Shreveport.	

	Yeah. It becomes a way bigger deal because my instincts are to just go for it. I’ve already accomplished so much given where I’ve come from, so just try your luck convincing me that I can’t do it, bro. I’m already convinced I can.
	
	
		You survived nine shots.	

	Tell me what’s left!

schema.headline: 50 Cent Opens Up About Diddy’s Secret Smear Campaign Against Him, Why He Won’t Work With Courtney Kemp Again and Learning His Mom Was Gay: ‘I’m Not Ashamed of That in Any Way’

title: Box Office: ‘Street Fighter’ Scores $13 Million Debut as ‘You Can See Everything’ Opens at No. 2 With $5.5 Million on Friday
description: “Street Fighter” punched its way to the top of the box office in a new-release-filled weekend, battling fellow openers “Sense and Sensibility,” “Wh
body:
“Street Fighter” punched its way to the top of the box office in a new-release-filled weekend, battling fellow openers “Sense and Sensibility,” “Whalefall” and “You Can See Everything.”

	The Paramount Pictures movie generated $13 million from 3,575 North American theaters on Friday. It’s a strong start for the action film, which looks to pull in $31 million by Sunday.


	“Street Fighter,” directed by Kitao Sakurai, stars Noah Centineo and Andrew Koji as two estranged fighters in the 90s who are recruited to enter a tournament that forces them to face off against each other. Based on the Capcom video game series, this iteration of “Street Fighter” is the third go-around for the IP — the first live-action film, released in 1994 and starring Jean-Claude Van Damme, was a box office hit with $100 million (not adjusted for inflation), while 2009’s “Street Fighter: The Legend of Chun-Li” earned just $12.8 million against a $50 million budget, becoming a major misfire for 20th Century.
	

	A24’s much-hyped Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” landed in second place on Friday, grossing $5.54 million on Friday from 855 North American theaters. Per rival estimates, the film looks to add $12.45 million by Sunday, exceeding initial estimates of a $7 to $8 million opening weekend. The documentary should overtake Amazon MGM’s “Melania,” which landed the biggest opening for a non-music or concert doc in over a decade with $7.1 million from 1,778 theaters.


	In the buzzy doc, comedian Nathan Fielder and “Primetime” filmmaker Lance Oppenheim quietly worked for more than three years on the movie, which offers an unhinged look at the Theranos founder a month before she began an 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors.
	

	Coming in right ahead of “Whalefall,” Focus Features’ “Sense and Sensibility” pulled in $3.3 million on Friday from 2,545 North American theaters, good enough for a third-place finish. The Georgia Oakley-directed remake of Jane Austen’s “Sense and Sensibility” is targeting a $6.7 million opening weekend.

	Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles star in the latest adaptation as sisters Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, who navigate love, loss and financial uncertainty as they are forced to leave their family estate in Sussex. The Austen classic has been adapted for the big screen numerous times, though the most notable one being the 1995 film starring Emma Thompson and Kate Winslet, which was both a critical and commercial hit.

	Disney’s survival thriller “Whalefall” took the No. 4 spot on Friday with $3 million from 2,065 locations. Rival estimates expect the survival thriller to bring in $7 million by Sunday. Directed by Brian Duffield, “Whalefall” follows a scuba diver (Austin Abrams) who is swallowed by a sperm whale and has only one hour of oxygen left in his tank as he figures out how to escape.

	Finally, in fifth was Universal’s “Other Mommy.” The supernatural horror grossed $2.5 million on Friday and should pull in another $7.85 million by Sunday, bringing its cumulative gross to $44.35 million.

	Based on Josh Malerman’s 2024 novel “Incidents Around the House,” the horror film follows a paranormal entity that takes on the appearance of a young girl’s mother and begins haunting their home. Chastain plays Ursula, the real mom, but also the titular “Other Mommy,” a terrifying entity who looks identical to Ursula.

Harry Styles
                          Honors Liam Payne With New Song ...
                          On Anniversary Of His Death
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 17, 2026

            Harry Styles paid tribute in a big way to Liam Payne during his Friday night gig at Madison Square Garden, belting out a special song he wrote in memory of his late former bandmate.
      
    
            Styles hit the stage at MSG in Midtown Manhattan for his latest performance Friday and to showcase his yet-to-be-released song, “What Is Enough," which Harry specifically wrote for Liam.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            As you know, the two were very close when they were members of the famous boy band, "One Direction," along with Niall Horan, Louis Tomlinson, and Zayn Malik.
      

            What made the moment even more poignant during Harry's MSG concert was that it marked the anniversary of Liam's untimely death. In October 2024, Liam fell to his death from a third-floor balcony at a hotel in Buenos Aires, Argentina.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            Before diving into the new song, Harry took a moment to talk to the sold-out crowd about Liam, saying that two years ago today he lost one of his closest friends.
      
    
            Harry continued ... “I’m sure a lot of you have been through similar things. I hope you haven’t. But really, it’s just about looking after each other.”
      
    
            He went on ... “So many people who have touched my life in such special ways. I wouldn’t be here without. I’m gonna play you a song I wrote for my friend about two years ago, if that’s all right.”
      
    
            Then Harry brought down the house with his live rendition of “What Is Enough,” honoring his late friend as the crowd went wild.

title: Six Flags Over Georgia: Halloween Show Renamed After Deadly Coaster Fall
description:
Six Flags Over Georgia
                          No More 'Dead Man's Party' ...
body:
Six Flags Over Georgia
                          No More 'Dead Man's Party' ...
                          After Fatal Coaster Fall
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 16, 2026
                            5:05 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Six Flags Over Georgia is taking the "dead" out of its Halloween festivities ... just days after a man plunged to his death from a roller coaster at the park.
      
    
            The theme park has quietly renamed its Fright Fest show "Dr. Fright's Dead Man's Party" to simply "Dr. Fright's Party" following Monday's horrific accident, according to the USA Today.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The change comes as Six Flags reopens Friday after shutting down for several days following the death of Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old Atlanta educator who was thrown from the Goliath roller coaster.
      

            And the name change isn't limited to Georgia ... the same show's listing at Six Flags Great Adventure in New Jersey has also been updated.
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported, Six Flags is moving forward with its "Final Destination"-themed Halloween attraction despite the deadly incident. The horror franchise famously features a gruesome roller coaster disaster in its third movie.
      
    
            The park previously told TMZ the attraction doesn't feature any theme park scenes.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Meanwhile, Goliath remains shut down as investigators work to determine how Hassan was ejected from the ride, striking other passengers and the tracks before landing beneath the coaster.
      
    
            Four children were also injured in the horrifying incident and taken to the hospital.
      
    
            So, while Six Flags is still serving up Halloween scares ... it appears the park is being a little more careful about how it sells them.
